title: Sovereign Debt Restructuring
issue: When a country can no longer service its foreign debt, its bonds are often restructured through negotiations between the government and private creditors. Some argue that an international bankruptcy court, operating under a binding treaty, should replace these ad hoc negotiations.

perspectives.label: Perspective One
perspectives.text: A binding international court would bring predictability. Creditors would know the rules in advance, holdout investors could no longer block deals that most creditors accept, and countries in distress would recover faster.

perspectives.label: Perspective Two
perspectives.text: Sovereign debt is ultimately a political matter. A court cannot compel a sovereign to pay, and any treaty would be ignored by the powerful states whose participation matters most. Contractual tools such as collective-action clauses already solve the holdout problem.

perspectives.label: Perspective Three
perspectives.text: The real risk is moral hazard. If restructuring becomes orderly and cheap, governments will borrow more recklessly, and lenders will demand higher interest from every developing country, punishing the prudent along with the profligate.

task: Write an argumentative essay in which you take a position on whether an international sovereign bankruptcy court should replace negotiated restructurings. In your essay, consider at least one of the perspectives above, and explain how your position relates to it.

title: Precedent and Constitutional Error
issue: Courts generally follow their own prior decisions (stare decisis). But when a high court becomes convinced that one of its earlier constitutional rulings was wrongly decided, it must choose between stability and correction.

perspectives.label: Perspective One
perspectives.text: A wrongly decided constitutional ruling should be overruled as soon as a court recognizes the error. Unlike statutes, constitutional rulings cannot easily be corrected by legislatures, so the court is the only remedy.

perspectives.label: Perspective Two
perspectives.text: The legitimacy of courts depends on the perception that law, not the shifting composition of the bench, decides cases. Overruling should require far more than a belief that the earlier case was wrong; it requires that the ruling has proven unworkable.

perspectives.label: Perspective Three
perspectives.text: Reliance is the decisive factor. Where people and institutions have arranged their affairs around a ruling, overruling it imposes real costs on those who trusted the courts, regardless of whether the original reasoning was sound.

task: Write an argumentative essay in which you take a position on when, if ever, a high court should overrule its own constitutional precedent. Engage with at least one of the perspectives above.

title: Language Requirements for Naturalization
issue: Many countries require applicants for citizenship to demonstrate proficiency in a national language. Critics argue that such requirements exclude long-term residents who contribute fully to society; supporters see them as essential to civic participation.

perspectives.label: Perspective One
perspectives.text: Citizenship carries the right to vote and serve on juries. Meaningful participation in public deliberation requires a shared language, so proficiency is a reasonable condition of citizenship.

perspectives.label: Perspective Two
perspectives.text: Language tests disproportionately burden older migrants and those who had limited schooling. A residence requirement alone better measures commitment to a country than a test that rewards prior privilege.

perspectives.label: Perspective Three
perspectives.text: Multilingual states function well without a single civic language. Rather than test applicants, governments should provide public materials in several languages and fund voluntary instruction.

task: Write an argumentative essay in which you take a position on whether language proficiency should be a requirement for naturalization. Address at least one of the perspectives above.

title: Disclosure of Climate Risk
issue: Securities regulators in several jurisdictions are considering whether to require publicly traded companies to disclose the financial risks they face from climate change, including the emissions associated with their operations.

perspectives.label: Perspective One
perspectives.text: Investors are entitled to information material to a company's value. Climate risk affects asset values, insurance costs, and regulation; mandatory, standardized disclosure prevents firms from hiding risks investors cannot otherwise assess.

perspectives.label: Perspective Two
perspectives.text: Climate projections are highly uncertain. Mandating disclosure of speculative estimates invites litigation, imposes compliance costs that fall hardest on smaller issuers, and gives investors false precision.

perspectives.label: Perspective Three
perspectives.text: Disclosure rules are the wrong tool for an environmental problem. Securities regulators should protect investors, not pursue policy goals that belong to legislatures and environmental agencies.

task: Write an argumentative essay in which you take a position on whether securities regulators should mandate climate-risk disclosure. Engage with at least one of the perspectives above.

title: Universal Jurisdiction
issue: Under the doctrine of universal jurisdiction, some national courts prosecute serious international crimes—such as genocide or torture—even when neither the crime, the victims, nor the accused have any connection to the prosecuting state.

perspectives.label: Perspective One
perspectives.text: Certain crimes offend all humanity. When the state where they occurred is unwilling or unable to prosecute, any court that can secure the accused should be able to try them; otherwise impunity prevails.

perspectives.label: Perspective Two
perspectives.text: Universal jurisdiction lets powerful states sit in judgment of weaker ones, inviting politically motivated prosecutions. International tribunals with broad membership are the only legitimate forum.

perspectives.label: Perspective Three
perspectives.text: Prosecutions far from the scene of the crime are costly, slow, and remote from the communities affected. Support for local justice institutions would do more good than trials in distant capitals.

task: Write an argumentative essay in which you take a position on whether national courts should exercise universal jurisdiction over international crimes. Address at least one of the perspectives above.
